detailed_description: The JWT Decoder helps developers inspect the visible parts of a JSON Web Token without setting up a local script. Paste a token into the input field and the page decodes the Base64URL header and payload, then displays the header, payload, raw signature segment, and claim table in a readable layout. It is useful for debugging authentication flows, checking whether expected claims such as sub, role, iat, or exp are present, and converting Unix-style expiration values into human-readable dates. The page is a decoder and inspection aid, not an authenticity checker: it does not ask for a secret or public key, and it does not prove that a token is trustworthy. Use it to understand token contents quickly, then check signatures and authorization rules in your application or security tooling.
usage_steps: Paste a JWT into the token input field.
Confirm the token has the expected three-part structure: header, payload, and signature.
Read the decoded header to check the token type and algorithm metadata.
Read the decoded payload and claim table to inspect user, role, issuer, issued-at, and expiration fields.
Use the copy buttons when you need to move the decoded header or payload into a bug report or local test case.
If an exp claim is present, review the displayed date to see whether the token is already expired.
usage_examples: A frontend developer checks whether a login response includes the expected role claim before enabling an admin-only screen.
A backend developer compares the payload from staging and production tokens while debugging an authorization mismatch.
A QA engineer pastes a sample token to confirm that the exp value lines up with a session timeout test case.
A support engineer reads non-sensitive claims from a test token to understand why a feature flag is not available.

faqs.question: Does this JWT Decoder verify signatures?
faqs.answer: No. It decodes and displays the token parts so you can inspect them. Cryptographic authenticity checks require the correct secret or public key and should be done in your application or trusted security tooling.

faqs.question: Can I paste production tokens into this page?
faqs.answer: Use caution. JWT payloads can contain account identifiers, roles, emails, or other sensitive claims. Prefer test tokens or redacted examples when possible.

faqs.question: What does an invalid format error mean?
faqs.answer: A standard JWT has three Base64URL sections separated by periods. If the token has fewer or more sections, or if a section cannot be decoded as JSON, the page reports an error.

faqs.question: Why can I read a JWT without a password?
faqs.answer: Most JWT headers and payloads are encoded, not encrypted. Decoding reveals their JSON content, but it does not prove the token is valid or authorized.

faqs.question: What should I check first in a decoded JWT?
faqs.answer: Start with issuer, audience, subject, issued-at time, expiration time, and role or permission claims. Then compare those values with what your application expects.
